## The strongest result is now a complete weak-dephasing prediction across a frequency band

I developed the opening into **a representation built from computable conservation defects**. It gives useful predictions even when the dephasing is weak, the interactions remain frustrated, and the relevant observable has no overlap with the single global-energy mode.

The strongest completed calculation is this:

\[
\boxed{
\left|F(\omega)-0.994097421306\right|
\le 0.004903577695
\qquad
\text{for every }|\omega|\le \frac1{4000}.
}
\]

Here \(F\) is a precisely specified, normalized infinite-temperature correlation spectrum of a **connected, frustrated 16,384-spin model**, with transverse drives \(100\) times the dephasing rate and physical linewidth \(\eta=10^{-5}\). The full input was read, the required operator coefficients were constructed, and the certificate was evaluated with exact integer and rational arithmetic. The complete calculation took about **3.14 seconds** in this runtime.

The continuum-band statement follows from three acquired polynomial coefficients. It does not use a frequency grid or extrapolation.

The broader physical consequence is also proved: **a driven probe coupled to an interacting quantum bath can have its integrated correlation certified from the noise-weighted current of the bath observable to which it couples**. Strong quantum exchange remains in the bath. I completed that calculation as well, including a source restricted to a fixed magnetization sector.

These results establish concrete capabilities and an organizing principle. They do **not** establish a general weak-noise simulator or a best-method advantage over existing methods supplied with the new correctors.
